claim: Viral transcription and progeny production are poorly correlated in single influenza virus-infected cells.
source: We find that viral transcription and progeny production are poorly correlated in single cells.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Cells that transcribe the most viral mRNA do not produce the most viral progeny.
source: The cells that transcribe the most viral mRNA do not produce the most viral progeny and often represent aberrant infections that fail to express the influenza NS gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5A and 5B showing poor correlation between transcription and progeny production.

claim: Cells with extremely high viral transcription often fail to express the NS gene and represent non-productive infections.
source: Instead, cells with extremely high viral transcription often fail to express the NS gene and represent non-productive infections.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing cells not expressing NS have significantly higher viral transcription.

claim: Only some of the discrepancy between transcription and progeny production can be explained by viral gene absence or mutations.
source: However, only some of the discrepancy between transcription and progeny production can be explained by viral gene absence or mutations: there is also a wide range of progeny production among cells infected by complete unmutated virions.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing heterogeneity in progeny production even among cells with complete unmutated genomes.

claim: Viral transcription is a relatively poor predictor of an infected cell's contribution to the progeny population.
source: Overall, our results show that viral transcription is a relatively poor predictor of an infected cell's contribution to the progeny population.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing poor correlation between transcription and progeny production.

claim: Individual infected cells vary widely in transcription of viral genes.
source: Individual infected cells vary widely in transcription of viral genes (Russell et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020; Zanini et al., 2018; Drayman et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Individual infected cells vary widely in expression of viral proteins.
source: Individual infected cells vary widely in...expression of viral proteins (Drayman et al., 2019; Brooke et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Individual infected cells vary widely in presence of viral mutations.
source: Individual infected cells vary widely in...presence of viral mutations (Russell et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 3.

claim: Individual infected cells vary widely in replication of viral genomes.
source: Individual infected cells vary widely in...replication of viral genomes (Schulte and Andino, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Individual infected cells vary widely in production of viral progeny.
source: Individual infected cells vary widely in...production of viral progeny (Zhu et al., 2009; Schulte and Andino, 2014; Delbrück, 1945; Heldt et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 4.

claim: The most common single-cell techniques measure the levels of proteins and transcripts, rather than the number of viral progeny produced.
source: The answer to this question remains elusive because the most common single-cell techniques (flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing) measure the levels of proteins and transcripts, rather than the number of viral progeny produced.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current techniques based on established knowledge of these methods.

claim: Progeny production is even more heterogeneous than viral transcription in single cells.
source: We find that progeny production is even more heterogeneous than viral transcription in single cells.
evidence: This is supported by Gini coefficients in Figure 4 showing higher values for progeny production (0.78, 0.87) than transcription (0.46, 0.40).

claim: Random nucleotide barcodes can be inserted into the influenza virus genome near the 3′ end of viral mRNAs.
source: To quantify the progeny virions released from single infected cells, we inserted random nucleotide barcodes (Lauring and Andino, 2011; Amato et al., 2022; Varble et al., 2014) into the influenza virus genome so that they are positioned near the 3′ end of the viral mRNAs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior work using barcoding approaches.

claim: Standard 3′-end single-cell sequencing of mRNA in infected cells captures the viral barcode sequence.
source: Standard 3′-end single-cell sequencing of the mRNA in infected cells (Russell et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020; Russell et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Steuerman et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2020) captures the viral barcode sequence, along with host and viral transcripts, enabling determination of which barcoded virion(s) infected each cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and citations to prior single-cell sequencing studies.

claim: Sequencing viral barcodes on progeny virions released into the supernatant can quantify the relative number of physical progeny produced by each cell.
source: We can sequence the viral barcodes on progeny virions released into the supernatant to quantify the relative number of physical progeny produced by each cell
evidence: This is part of the experimental design described and implemented in the study.

claim: Sequencing viral barcodes in cells secondarily infected with supernatant can quantify the relative number of infectious progeny produced by each cell.
source: sequence the viral barcodes in cells secondarily infected with an aliquot of the supernatant to quantify the relative number of infectious progeny produced by each cell
evidence: This is part of the experimental design described and implemented in the study.

claim: The genome of the virion that infected each cell can be reconstructed by selectively amplifying viral genes from the single-cell cDNA library and performing long-read sequencing.
source: Additionally, we can reconstruct the genome of the virion that infected each cell by selectively amplifying viral genes from the single-cell cDNA library and performing long-read sequencing as described previously (Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the methods described and citation to prior work, with data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Barcodes were inserted near the 3′ end of the mRNA sequence between the stop codon and the polyA site.
source: Barcodes were inserted near the 3′ end of the mRNA sequence between the stop codon and the polyA site, using a duplicated packaging signal scheme to avoid disrupting viral genome packaging.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the methods.

claim: A duplicated packaging signal scheme was used to avoid disrupting viral genome packaging.
source: using a duplicated packaging signal scheme to avoid disrupting viral genome packaging
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the methods, with citations to prior work (Heaton et al., 2013; Gao and Palese, 2009).

claim: Viruses with one or two barcoded segments grew to similar titers as viruses with unmodified genomes.
source: Viruses with one or two barcoded segments grew to similar titers as viruses with unmodified genomes. The titers shown were measured after generating the viruses by transfection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with experimental data comparing titers.

claim: The frequencies of viral barcodes were fairly consistent across passages, indicating a lack of selection for any particular barcode sequence.
source: The frequencies of viral barcodes were fairly consistent across passages, indicating a lack of selection for any particular barcode sequence.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with experimental data.

claim: In a sample of 1500 barcodes from the virus library, >96% of barcodes were unique for both HA and NA.
source: We used deep sequencing to verify that for both HA and NA, in a sample of 1500 barcodes from our virus library, >96% of barcodes were unique (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 with rarefaction curve analysis.

claim: In a sample of 4000 barcodes, >92% were unique.
source: In a sample of 4000 barcodes, >92% were unique (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 with rarefaction curve analysis.

claim: For the low MOI condition, approximately 10,000 MDCK-SIAT1-TMPRSS2 cells were infected with the dual-barcoded virus library at an MOI of approximately 0.15.
source: For the low MOI condition, we infected ~104 MDCK-SIAT1-TMPRSS2 cells (Lee et al., 2018) with the dual-barcoded virus library at an MOI of ~0.15
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: At low MOI, most cells are uninfected, and most infected cells are infected by a single virion.
source: under these conditions, most cells are uninfected, and most infected cells are infected by a single virion
evidence: This is an inference based on the MOI of 0.15 and established knowledge of Poisson distribution of viral infection.

claim: For the high MOI conditions, approximately 7,000 cells were infected at an MOI of approximately 0.6.
source: For the high MOI conditions, we infected ~7 × 103 cells at an MOI of ~0.6
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: At high MOI, fewer cells are uninfected and a substantial fraction of the infected cells are infected by multiple virions.
source: under these conditions, fewer cells are uninfected and a substantial fraction of the infected cells are infected by multiple virions
evidence: This is an inference based on the MOI of 0.6 and established knowledge of Poisson distribution of viral infection.

claim: The virus inoculum was replaced with fresh medium after 1 hr and ammonium chloride was added to prevent secondary infection.
source: To ensure a single round of relatively synchronized infection, we replaced the virus inoculum with fresh medium after 1 hr and added ammonium chloride, which prevents secondary infection by blocking the endosomal acidification necessary for viral fusion (Martin and Helenius, 1991; Ohkuma and Poole, 1978).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol with citations supporting the mechanism of ammonium chloride.

claim: Ammonium chloride prevents secondary infection by blocking the endosomal acidification necessary for viral fusion.
source: ammonium chloride, which prevents secondary infection by blocking the endosomal acidification necessary for viral fusion (Martin and Helenius, 1991; Ohkuma and Poole, 1978)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work establishing this mechanism.

claim: Cells were collected for single-cell RNA sequencing at 12 hr after infection.
source: We collected the cells for single-cell RNA sequencing at a single timepoint 12 hr after infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For the low MOI sample, single-cell RNA sequencing data was obtained for 254 cells infected with the barcoded virus library.
source: For the low MOI sample, we obtained single-cell RNA sequencing data for 254 cells infected with our barcoded virus library
evidence: This reports the number of cells analyzed in the experiment.

claim: The empirical MOI for the low MOI sample was 0.17.
source: resulting in an empirical MOI of 0.17 (since we recovered data for ~1600 total cells from this sample)
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: For the high MOI sample, single-cell RNA sequencing data was obtained for 357 cells infected with the barcoded virus library.
source: For the high MOI sample, we obtained single-cell RNA sequencing data for 357 cells infected with our barcoded virus library
evidence: This reports the number of cells analyzed in the experiment.

claim: The empirical MOI for the high MOI sample was approximately 0.59.
source: resulting in an empirical MOI of ~0.59 (since we recovered data for ~800 total cells from this sample)
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: Many cells are lost during preparation for single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: Note that many cells are lost during preparation for single-cell RNA sequencing, so an important caveat of our study is that some infected cells that produced viral progeny are absent in the transcriptome data (Zheng et al., 2017; Yamawaki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a known limitation of single-cell RNA sequencing supported by citations.

claim: Under both infection conditions, there was extremely wide variation in the amount of viral transcription among infected cells.
source: Under both infection conditions, there was extremely wide variation in the amount of viral transcription among infected cells (Figure 2A), similar to that observed in prior single-cell studies of influenza infection (Russell et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020; Russell et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Steuerman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In most infected cells, viral transcripts accounted for <10% of all transcripts.
source: In most infected cells, viral transcripts accounted for <10% of all transcripts
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In a small number of cells, over half of the transcripts were derived from virus.
source: but in a small number of cells, over half of the transcripts were derived from virus (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: On average, cells infected at high MOI expressed higher levels of viral transcripts than cells infected at low MOI.
source: On average, cells infected at high MOI expressed higher levels of viral transcripts than cells infected at low MOI, but there was extensive variation under both conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A comparing the two MOI conditions.

claim: Under low MOI conditions, approximately 40% of the infected cells failed to express all eight viral genes.
source: Under low MOI conditions, a substantial fraction (~40%) of the infected cells also failed to express all eight viral genes (Figure 2B), a phenomenon that has been extensively described in prior studies (Russell et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020; Brooke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Under high MOI conditions, fewer cells failed to express all eight viral genes.
source: Under high MOI conditions, fewer cells failed to express all eight viral genes (Figure 2B), likely because of complementation by co-infection (Phipps et al., 2020; Jacobs et al., 2019; Sims et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and the explanation is supported by citations to prior work on complementation.

claim: Each viral gene was not expressed in some infected cells, with variation between the rates of absence for each specific gene.
source: At a per gene level, each viral gene was not expressed in some infected cells, with variation between the rates of absence for each specific gene (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Complete sequences of all expressed viral genes were obtained for 131 of the 254 infected cells in the low MOI dataset.
source: We obtained complete sequences of all expressed viral genes for 131 of the 254 infected cells in our low MOI dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This reports the sequencing coverage achieved in the experiment.

claim: About a third of the infected cells expressed all eight viral genes without any non-synonymous mutations.
source: About a third of the infected cells expressed all eight viral genes without any non-synonymous mutations (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The remainder of infected cells failed to express a viral gene, expressed a gene with a non-synonymous mutation, or both.
source: The remainder of infected cells failed to express a viral gene, expressed a gene with a non-synonymous mutation, or both (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutated virions most commonly had just one non-synonymous mutation in their genome, but some virions had two or three mutations.
source: Mutated virions most commonly had just one non-synonymous mutation in their genome, but some virions had two or three mutations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Some virions had large internal deletions in a gene.
source: Note that some virions had large internal deletions in a gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) as has been previously described (Saira et al., 2013; Davis et al., 1980)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The number of progeny virions produced per cell was extremely heterogeneous at both low MOI and high MOI.
source: The number of progeny virions produced per cell was extremely heterogeneous at both low MOI and high MOI (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Under low MOI conditions, nearly half of the infected cells failed to produce any detectable physical or infectious progeny.
source: Under low MOI conditions, nearly half of the infected cells failed to produce any detectable physical or infectious progeny.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: At the extreme high end of viral transcription, a few cells each generated >10% of all the virions detected in the progeny population.
source: At the extreme high end of viral transcription, a few cells each generated >10% of all the virions detected in the progeny population (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: At high MOI, the most productive cells generated a smaller fraction of progeny than at low MOI.
source: A similar trend was seen at high MOI, although under these conditions the most productive cells generated a smaller fraction of progeny (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A comparing the two MOI conditions.

claim: Just 6 of 91 infected cells were responsible for generating half of the physical progeny at low MOI.
source: While just 6 of 91 infected cells were responsible for generating half of the physical progeny at low MOI, 23 cells were required to account for half of the viral transcripts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 23 cells were required to account for half of the viral transcripts at low MOI.
source: While just 6 of 91 infected cells were responsible for generating half of the physical progeny at low MOI, 23 cells were required to account for half of the viral transcripts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under low MOI conditions, the Gini coefficients were 0.78 and 0.88 for physical and infectious progeny production.
source: Under low MOI conditions, the Gini coefficients were 0.78 and 0.88 for physical and infectious progeny production (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: At high MOI, the Gini coefficient for physical progeny production was 0.66.
source: At high MOI, heterogeneity was reduced slightly and the Gini coefficient for physical progeny production was 0.66 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Gini coefficients for viral transcription were 0.46 at low MOI and 0.40 at high MOI.
source: The Gini coefficients for viral transcription were 0.46 at low MOI and 0.40 at high MOI (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Gini coefficients for viral transcription are lower than the corresponding coefficients for progeny production.
source: both of which are lower than the corresponding coefficients for progeny production
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the Gini coefficients reported in Figure 4.

claim: The correlation between viral transcription and progeny production in single cells is surprisingly poor at both low MOI and high MOI.
source: The correlation between viral transcription and progeny production in single cells is surprisingly poor at both low MOI and high MOI (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Under low MOI conditions, none of the cells with >25% of their mRNA transcripts derived from virus produce any detectable progeny.
source: Under low MOI conditions, none of the cells with >25% of their mRNA transcripts derived from virus produce any detectable progeny (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Most progeny come from cells with moderate viral transcription at low MOI.
source: Instead, most progeny come from cells with moderate viral transcription.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At high MOI, viral progeny are produced by cells throughout the range of viral transcription.
source: At high MOI, viral progeny are produced by cells throughout the range of viral transcription (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is no trend for cells with high transcription to produce more progeny even at high MOI.
source: but there is no trend for cells with high transcription to produce more progeny even at high MOI
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells that fail to express any viral gene produce little or no detectable progeny virions, regardless of their total viral transcription activity.
source: Cells that fail to express any viral gene produce little or no detectable progeny virions, regardless of their total viral transcription activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The lack of physical progeny produced by cells that fail to express even a single viral gene presumably occurs because the absence of the encoded protein impairs virion formation.
source: The lack of physical progeny produced by cells that fail to express even a single viral gene presumably occurs because the absence of the encoded protein impairs virion formation (Figure 5D; note that our analysis is limited to cells that express HA and NA since those are the barcoded genes).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known requirement for all viral proteins in virion formation.

claim: Cells that express the full complement of viral genes often still fail to produce detectable progeny.
source: But although cells that fail to express a viral gene produce little or no progeny, the converse is not true: cells that express the full complement of viral genes often still fail to produce detectable progeny (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Absence of the influenza NS gene not only precludes progeny production but is specifically associated with an aberrant state of high viral transcription.
source: Strikingly, absence of the influenza NS gene not only precludes progeny production but is specifically associated with an aberrant state of high viral transcription (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At both low MOI and high MOI, many of the highest transcribing cells fail to express NS.
source: At both low MOI and high MOI, many of the highest transcribing cells fail to express NS
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The mean level of viral transcription is significantly higher (p<0.01) in cells that do not express NS compared to cells that express all viral genes.
source: and the mean level of viral transcription is significantly higher (p<0.01) in cells that do not express NS compared to cells that express all viral genes (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with statistical testing described in the methods.

claim: NS acts as a negative regulator of viral transcription.
source: These data suggest that NS acts as a negative regulator of viral transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells lacking NS have higher transcription.

claim: The NEP protein expressed from the NS gene exports viral ribonucleoprotein complexes from the nucleus.
source: This observation is consistent with the known functional roles of the NEP protein expressed from the NS gene, which is to export viral ribonucleoprotein complexes from the nucleus (O'Neill et al., 1998; Bullido et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NEP may switch the viral polymerase from transcription to genome replication through direct protein–protein interactions.
source: and possibly to switch the viral polymerase from transcription to genome replication through direct protein–protein interactions (Robb et al., 2009; Mänz et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The cells that contribute the most to the signal observed in transcriptomic studies often represent aberrant non-productive infections that do not contribute viral progeny.
source: Overall, this result suggests that the cells that contribute the most to the signal observed in transcriptomic studies often represent aberrant non-productive infections that do not contribute viral progeny.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that high-transcribing cells often lack NS and produce no progeny.

claim: At low MOI, physical viral progeny are produced both by cells that express viral genes with mutations and by cells that express unmutated viral genes.
source: At low MOI, physical viral progeny are produced both by cells that express viral genes with mutations and by cells that express unmutated viral genes
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: More of the infectious progeny virions come from cells with unmutated viral genomes.
source: however, more of the infectious progeny virions come from cells with unmutated viral genomes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some non-synonymous mutations interfere with protein functions that are required for infection of new cells.
source: probably because some non-synonymous mutations interfere with protein functions that are required for infection of new cells
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the observation that mutated genomes produce less infectious progeny.

claim: Physical and infectious progeny production are much more correlated among single cells than are transcription and progeny production.
source: Nonetheless, physical and infectious progeny production are much more correlated among single cells than are transcription and progeny production (Figure 5A versus Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Pearson's R values of –0.14 for the correlation of transcription with infectious progeny at low MOI versus 0.39 for the correlation of physical progeny with infectious progeny at low MOI).
evidence: This is shown by comparing correlations in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the viral factors measured (viral transcription, expression of each viral gene, or mutated viral proteins) fully explain the extreme variation observed in progeny production.
source: However, none of the viral factors we measure (viral transcription, expression of each viral gene, or mutated viral proteins) fully explain the extreme variation we observe in progeny production.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that variation persists even after accounting for these factors.

claim: Progeny production remains highly variable across cells without any viral deficit.
source: Progeny production remains highly variable across cells without any viral deficit (e.g. cells that express unmutated copies of all viral genes), although it is less variable across this population than across all cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Cellular or uncharacterized viral factors must also contribute to cell-to-cell variation in progeny production.
source: This unexplained variation suggests that cellular or uncharacterized viral factors must also contribute to cell-to-cell variation in progeny production.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that known viral factors do not fully explain the variation.

claim: Prior single-cell studies of infection have examined intracellular viral products, like mRNA transcripts or proteins.
source: Most prior single-cell studies of infection have examined intracellular viral products, like mRNA transcripts or proteins (Russell et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020; Zanini et al., 2018; Drayman et al., 2019; Brooke et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2009; Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The most important outcome of infection for multi-cycle viral growth is how many progeny virions are produced by an infected cell.
source: However, the most important outcome of infection for multi-cycle viral growth is how many progeny virions are produced by an infected cell.
evidence: This is a statement based on established understanding of viral replication dynamics.

claim: Prior studies of progeny production from single cells have relied on isolating individual infected cells in small volumes.
source: Prior studies of progeny production from single cells have relied on isolating individual infected cells in small volumes (Zhu et al., 2009; Schulte and Andino, 2014; Delbrück, 1945; Heldt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prior studies have shown progeny production is highly heterogeneous, but have not provided measurements of most other properties of the infected cells.
source: These studies have shown progeny production is highly heterogeneous, but have not provided measurements of most other properties of the infected cells – and have therefore lacked explanatory power to understand the basis for the variation in progeny production.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Part of the discrepancy between transcription and progeny production is due to the fact that cells that fail to express the influenza NS gene tend to transcribe very high levels of mRNA but produce no progeny.
source: Part of the discrepancy between these two single-cell measurements is due to the fact that cells that fail to express the influenza NS gene tend to transcribe very high levels of mRNA but produce no progeny.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: One of the proteins encoded by the NS gene is NEP, which exports viral ribonucleoproteins from the nucleus.
source: This result makes biological sense: one of the proteins encoded by the NS gene is NEP, which exports viral ribonucleoproteins from the nucleus (O'Neill et al., 1998), terminating their transcriptional activity (Bullido et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NEP terminates the transcriptional activity of viral ribonucleoproteins.
source: terminating their transcriptional activity (Bullido et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NEP may mediate a switch from transcription to genome replication by the viral polymerase.
source: NEP may also mediate a switch from transcription to genome replication by the viral polymerase (Robb et al., 2009; Mänz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Absence of NS and other defects in the viral genome only explains part of the discordance between viral transcription and progeny production in single influenza-infected cells.
source: However, absence of NS and other defects in the viral genome only explains part of the discordance between viral transcription and progeny production in single influenza-infected cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that variation persists even in cells with complete unmutated genomes.

claim: Transcription and progeny production are often discordant even in cells expressing unmutated copies of all influenza genes.
source: These two properties are often discordant even in cells expressing unmutated copies of all influenza genes.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The experiments used a cell line rather than the differentiated airway cells that are the actual target cells during human influenza infections.
source: Our experiments used a cell line rather than the differentiated airway cells that are the actual target cells during human influenza infections.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system used.

claim: Experiments were performed using a single strain of H1N1 influenza at a single timepoint.
source: We performed experiments using a single strain of H1N1 influenza at a single timepoint.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing captures only a fraction of the input cells.
source: We were also able to profile all relevant single-cell properties for a relatively modest number of infected cells since single-cell RNA sequencing captures only a fraction of the input cells.
evidence: This is a known limitation of single-cell RNA sequencing technology.

claim: The method described should be extensible to other cell-culture systems and larger numbers of cells in future work.
source: However, the method we have described should be extensible to other cell-culture systems and larger numbers of cells in future work.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: Recent studies have examined the distribution of influenza virus transcription or protein expression across differentiated airway cells ex vivo.
source: First, recent studies have examined the distribution of influenza virus transcription or protein expression across differentiated airway cells ex vivo (Yamawaki et al., 2021; Kelly et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020) or in vivo (Steuerman et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2020; Hamele et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is important to measure progeny production across airway cells as the cell types expressing the most viral transcripts or proteins may not be the ones producing the most viral progeny.
source: Our results suggest it is also important to measure progeny production across airway cells as the cell types expressing the most viral transcripts or proteins may not be the ones producing the most viral progeny.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Failure of some cells to express specific viral genes contributes to the discordance between viral transcription and progeny production.
source: Second, our results suggest failure of some cells to express specific viral genes contributes to the discordance between viral transcription and progeny production.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Failure to express the influenza NS gene is strongly correlated with high viral transcription, even under high MOI conditions that promote genetic complementation.
source: Failure to express the influenza NS gene is strongly correlated with high viral transcription, even under high MOI conditions that promote genetic complementation (Phipps et al., 2020; Jacobs et al., 2019; Sims et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C and citations to prior work on complementation.

claim: Recent work on the transmission of influenza virus in humans has emphasized the narrow genetic bottleneck.
source: Third, recent work on the transmission of influenza virus (McCrone et al., 2018; Xue and Bloom, 2019) and SARS-CoV-2 (Braun et al., 2021; Martin and Koelle, 2021; Lythgoe et al., 2021) in humans has emphasized the narrow genetic bottleneck, with only a small fraction of viral diversity in the donor transmitted to the recipient.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent work on the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 in humans has emphasized the narrow genetic bottleneck.
source: Third, recent work on the transmission of influenza virus (McCrone et al., 2018; Xue and Bloom, 2019) and SARS-CoV-2 (Braun et al., 2021; Martin and Koelle, 2021; Lythgoe et al., 2021) in humans has emphasized the narrow genetic bottleneck, with only a small fraction of viral diversity in the donor transmitted to the recipient.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Only a small fraction of viral diversity in the donor is transmitted to the recipient during transmission.
source: with only a small fraction of viral diversity in the donor transmitted to the recipient
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on transmission bottlenecks.

claim: Physical bottlenecks in how many virions reach the recipient may be further narrowed by the fact that only a small fraction of the initially infected cells will produce most of the progeny that continue the infection.
source: Our results suggest physical bottlenecks in how many virions reach the recipient may be further narrowed by the fact that only a small fraction of the initially infected cells will produce most of the progeny that continue the infection.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings about heterogeneous progeny production.

claim: The HA segment of the A/California/04/2009 (pdmH1N1) strain of influenza virus with the G155E cell-culture adaptation mutation was engineered to carry exogenous sequence by duplicating the packaging signals at each end.
source: The HA segment of the A/California/04/2009 (pdmH1N1) strain of influenza virus with the G155E cell-culture adaptation mutation was engineered to carry exogenous sequence by duplicating the packaging signals at each end (Heaton et al., 2013; Gao and Palese, 2009), as schematized in Figure 1B.
evidence: This describes the engineering approach with citations to prior work.

claim: The G155E mutation greatly enhances viral growth in cell culture.
source: We included the G155E mutation as it greatly enhances viral growth in cell culture (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The terminal 105 nucleotides of the HA coding sequence were duplicated to provide an authentic packaging signal at the 5′ end of the vRNA.
source: The terminal 105 nucleotides of the HA coding sequence were duplicated to provide an authentic packaging signal at the 5′ end of the vRNA.
evidence: This describes the engineering approach.

claim: The corresponding 105 nucleotides of the HA protein coding sequence were synonymously recoded to remove competing RNA-RNA interactions.
source: The corresponding 105 nucleotides of the HA protein coding sequence were synonymously recoded to remove competing RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This describes the engineering approach.

claim: A second stop codon (TGA) was added at the end of the coding sequence to reduce the chance of translation read-through.
source: A second stop codon (TGA) was added at the end of the coding sequence to reduce the chance of translation read-through.
evidence: This describes the engineering approach.

claim: The stop codons were followed by an exogenous sequence containing a priming site, a 16-nucleotide random barcode, a second priming site, and a HindIII restriction site.
source: The stop codons were followed by an exogenous sequence containing a priming site, a 16-nucleotide random barcode, a second priming site, and a HindIII restriction site.
evidence: This describes the engineering approach.

claim: For the NA segment, 99 nucleotides at the 5′ end of the vRNA and 93 nucleotides at the 3′ end of the vRNA were duplicated.
source: The NA segment of the A/California/04/2009 strain was engineered using the same strategy except we duplicated 99 nucleotides at the 5′ end of the vRNA and 93 nucleotides at the 3′ end of the vRNA.
evidence: This describes the engineering approach for NA.

claim: Virus was generated by reverse genetics in 39 independent transfection reactions.
source: Virus was generated by reverse genetics in 39 independent transfection reactions.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For each transfection reaction, 4e5 293T cells were seeded in a well of a 6-well dish.
source: For each transfection reaction, 4e5 293T cells (ATCC #CRL-3216) were seeded in a well of a 6-well dish.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The virus library was passaged at low MOI to ensure a genotype–phenotype link between the viral genome and the proteins displayed on the surface of each virion.
source: To ensure a genotype–phenotype link between the viral genome and the proteins displayed on the surface of each virion, the virus library was passaged at low MOI.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: Infections were done at large scale to maintain library diversity.
source: Infections were done at large scale to maintain library diversity.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: A control sample of cells infected with an otherwise isogenic influenza virus carrying identifying synonymous mutations on all eight viral genes was used to estimate technical error rates.
source: The control cells were infected with an otherwise isogenic influenza virus that carried identifying synonymous mutations on all eight viral genes. The synonymous mutations are detectable by sequencing. They mark each mRNA transcript and genome segment derived from the virus library with a distinct 'genetic tag.'
evidence: This describes the experimental design for quality control.

claim: Genetic tags provide a means to detect transcriptomes that are derived from droplets that encapsulated multiple infected cells (multiplets).
source: First, in the single-cell RNA sequencing data, these tags provide a means to detect transcriptomes that are derived from droplets that encapsulated multiple infected cells (multiplets) (Bloom, 2018).
evidence: This describes the use of genetic tags for quality control with citation.

claim: Transcriptomes bearing both genetic tags are marked by high frequencies of both tags among the viral transcripts.
source: Such transcriptomes are marked by high frequencies of both tags among the viral transcripts.
evidence: This describes how multiplets are identified.

claim: Genetic tags are detectable in the long-read viral sequencing data used to reconstruct the genotype of infecting virions.
source: Second, the genetic tags are also detectable in the long-read viral sequencing data (Russell et al., 2019) we used to reconstruct the genotype of infecting virions.
evidence: This describes the use of genetic tags in long-read sequencing with citation.

claim: A polymerase can move from one template molecule to another in the midst of synthesizing its product, a phenomenon known as 'strand exchange'.
source: In the course of preparing long-read sequencing libraries, a polymerase can move from one template molecule to another in the midst of synthesizing its product – a phenomenon known as 'strand exchange' (Judo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Strand exchange can be detected in long-read viral sequences that contain discordant genetic tags.
source: This phenomenon can be detected in long-read viral sequences that contain discordant genetic tags (see Figure S10 of Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For the low MOI sample, 1500 transcriptionally active units of dual-barcoded virus library were added to the cells.
source: The medium was aspirated, and 1500 transcriptionally active units (measured by single-cell RNA sequencing) of dual-barcoded virus library in 100 μl of Influenza Growth Medium were added to the well.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For the high MOI sample, 4000 transcriptionally active units of dual-barcoded virus library were used to infect the cells.
source: The following changes were employed: 6.7 × 103 MDCK-SIAT1-TMPRSS2 cells (Lee et al., 2018) were plated and the cells were infected with 4000 transcriptionally active units (measured by single-cell RNA sequencing) of dual-barcoded virus library.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The template-switching oligo was replaced with a modified single-stranded DNA oligo to accommodate some of the barcoded influenza segments' exogenous sequence which shares homology with the standard 10× template-switching oligo.
source: The template-switching oligo was replaced with a modified single-stranded DNA oligo with the sequence 5′-AGAGTGTTTGGGTAGAGCAGCGTGTTGGCATGTrGrGrG-3′ at a final concentration of 45 µM in the reaction mix. This change was made to accommodate some of the barcoded influenza segments' exogenous sequence which shares homology with the standard 10× template-switching oligo.
evidence: This describes a modification to the standard protocol.

claim: The cDNA amplification PCR reaction extension time was increased to 20 s to encourage the formation of full-length cDNA products.
source: The cDNA amplification PCR reaction extension time was increased to 20 s to encourage the formation of full-length cDNA products.
evidence: This describes a modification to the standard protocol.

claim: For the low MOI sample, half of the amplified cDNA product was used as template for long-read sequencing of viral transcripts.
source: The amplified cDNA product was split in half. One half was used for fragmentation and preparation of the transcriptome sequencing library while, for the low MOI sample, the other half was used as template for long-read sequencing of viral transcripts.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Viral cDNA molecules were selectively enriched using a method described previously.
source: To capture these sequences, we selectively enriched viral cDNA molecules using a method described previously (Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the method with citation to prior work.

claim: Fewer than 1% of sequences were affected by strand exchange during sequencing library preparation.
source: We measured the rate of strand exchange that occurred during sequencing library preparation (see Figure S10 of Russell et al., 2019) and found that fewer than 1% of sequences were affected
evidence: This reports the measured rate of a technical artifact.

claim: Physical progeny virions were quantified by sequencing the vRNA in the viral supernatant at 12 hr post infection.
source: To quantify physical progeny virions, we sequenced the vRNA in the viral supernatant at 12 hr post infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For the low MOI sample, infectious progeny virions were quantified by infecting a second set of cells to select for virions that could perform viral entry and genome replication and sequencing the intracellular vRNA molecules at 13 hr post infection.
source: For the low MOI sample, to quantify infectious progeny virions, we infected a second set of cells to select for virions that could perform viral entry and genome replication (Figure 1A) and sequenced the intracellular vRNA molecules at 13 hr post infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Frozen viral supernatants collected at 12 hr post infection were split into four equal volumes.
source: In detail, we thawed frozen viral supernatants that were collected at 12 hr post infection and split them into four equal volumes.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Two volumes were used to isolate supernatant RNA directly.
source: Two volumes were used to isolate supernatant RNA directly.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For the low MOI sample, the other two volumes were used to infect MDCK-SIAT1-TMPRSS2 cells at a moderate estimated MOI of approximately 0.25 in two independent replicates.
source: For the low MOI sample, the other two volumes were used to infect MDCK-SIAT1-TMPRSS2 cells (Lee et al., 2018) at a moderate estimated MOI of ~0.25 in two independent replicates.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: RNA was isolated from the viral supernatant or infected cell pellets using the RNeasy Mini Kit.
source: RNA was isolated from the viral supernatant or infected cell pellets using the RNeasy Mini Kit (QIAGEN, 74104).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Reverse transcription was performed with a segment-specific primer targeted to the HA or NA vRNA.
source: Reverse transcription was performed with a segment-specific primer targeted to the HA or NA vRNA (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Two replicate reactions were performed using RNA from the viral supernatant sample, and two independent reactions were performed using RNA from the two infected cell pellets.
source: Two replicate reactions were performed using RNA from the viral supernatant sample, and two independent reactions were performed using RNA from the two infected cell pellets; these replicates provide technical duplicate measurements of both the physical progeny in the supernatant and the infectious progeny in the cell pellets.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Viral barcodes were amplified in 50 μl PCR reactions using KOD Hot-Start Master Mix.
source: Viral barcodes were amplified in 50 μl PCR reactions using KOD Hot-Start Master Mix (Sigma-Aldrich, 71842).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Amplicons were size-selected and purified using a double-sided AmpureXP bead cleanup.
source: Amplicons were size-selected and purified using a double-sided AmpureXP bead cleanup.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Sequencing indices and adapters were attached in a 50 μl PCR reaction using KOD Hot-Start Master Mix.
source: Sequencing indices and adapters were attached in a 50 μl PCR reaction using KOD Hot-Start Master Mix.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The resulting amplicons were gel-purified and pooled for single-end sequencing on an Illumina MiSeq.
source: The resulting amplicons were gel-purified and pooled for single-end sequencing on an Illumina MiSeq.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: A reproducible pipeline that performs all analysis is available at https://github.com/jbloomlab/barcoded_flu_pdmH1N1.
source: A reproducible pipeline that performs all analysis is available at https://github.com/jbloomlab/barcoded_flu_pdmH1N1.
evidence: This provides information about data availability.

claim: The pipeline uses Snakemake.
source: The pipeline uses Snakemake (Köster and Rahmann, 2012).
evidence: This describes the computational tools used with citation.

claim: The raw sequencing data from the single-cell RNA sequencing was aligned using STARsolo Version 2.7.6a.
source: Briefly, the raw sequencing data from the single-cell RNA sequencing was aligned using STARsolo RRID:SCR_021542 Version 2.7.6a (Kaminow et al., 2021)
evidence: This describes the computational analysis with citation.

claim: Alignment was performed against a composite reference made up of the canine genome CanFam3.1.98 concatenated to the A/California/04/2009 influenza virus genome.
source: against a composite reference made up of the canine genome CanFam3.1.98 concatenated to the A/California/04/2009 influenza virus genome
evidence: This describes the computational analysis.

claim: For the low MOI sample, cells were called as infected if at least 1% of their transcripts came from virus.
source: For the low MOI sample, cells were called as infected if at least 1% of their transcripts came from virus.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis criteria.

claim: For the high MOI sample, cells were called as infected if at least 2.5% of their transcripts came from virus.
source: For the high MOI sample, cells were called as infected if at least 2.5% of their transcripts came from virus.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis criteria.

claim: Individual viral genes were called as expressed if their frequency was greater than the 99th percentile observed in uninfected cells.
source: Individual viral genes were called as expressed if their frequency was greater than the 99th percentile observed in uninfected cells (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the computational analysis criteria.

claim: A non-parametric permutation test was performed with 5000 permutations to test for statistical significance in Figure 5C.
source: Because the data are not normally distributed, we performed a non-parametric permutation test, randomly labeling each observed value with a classification. We performed 5000 permutations and calculated the p-value as the frequency with which the randomly generated difference between classified groups matched or exceeded the observed difference between groups.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis performed.

claim: Cells missing the NS gene have a statistically significant difference in viral transcription compared to cells that express all viral genes (p<0.01) under both low MOI and high MOI conditions.
source: The results indicated that cells missing the NS gene have a statistically significant difference in viral transcription compared to cells that express all viral genes (p<0.01) under both low MOI and high MOI conditions.
evidence: This reports the results of statistical testing.

claim: Consensus sequences were generated from the subread files, requiring a minimum accuracy (rq) of 0.99 for the consensus sequence.
source: For the low MOI sample, the raw PacBio sequencing data was processed using PacBio's ccs program RRID:SCR_021174 Version 5.0.0 (https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/ccs; PacBio, 2022). Consensus sequences were generated from the subread files, requiring a minimum accuracy (`rq`) of 0.99 for the consensus sequence.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis.

claim: A mutation was included in the consensus sequence if it was found in >50% of the CCS for the cell barcode–viral gene–UMI combination.
source: A mutation was included in the consensus sequence if it was found in >50% of the CCS for the cell barcode–viral gene–UMI combination.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis criteria.

claim: A mutation was included in the final consensus sequence if it was found in >50% of the UMIs for the cell barcode–viral gene and was found in at least two UMIs.
source: A consensus sequence was then called for each cell barcode–viral gene combination. A mutation was included in the consensus sequence if it was found in >50% of the UMIs for the cell barcode–viral gene and was found in at least two UMIs.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis criteria.

claim: The viral barcodes were error-corrected using UMI-tools Version 1.1.0.
source: The viral barcodes were error-corrected using UMI-tools RRID:SCR_017048 Version 1.1.0 (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the computational analysis with citation.

claim: The limit of detection was set at 1e-5, where viral barcode frequencies fail to correlate, indicating bottlenecked subsampling of the molecules carrying the viral barcodes.
source: The technical replicates for each sample were plotted against each other and the limit of detection was set at 1e-5, where viral barcode frequencies fail to correlate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating bottlenecked subsampling of the molecules carrying the viral barcodes, and suggesting that frequency measurements below this threshold are not reliable
evidence: This describes the computational analysis criteria with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Values below the limit of detection were set to the limit of detection.
source: values below the limit of detection were set to the limit of detection
evidence: This describes the computational analysis approach.

claim: To determine the fraction of progeny contributed by each infected cell, the geometric mean of the HA and NA barcode frequencies associated with each cell was taken.
source: To determine the fraction of progeny contributed by each infected cell in this set, we took the geometric mean of the HA and NA barcode frequencies associated with each cell.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis approach.

claim: Progeny contributions were normalized by the total frequencies assignable to any cell in the analyzed set.
source: We normalized the progeny contributions by the total frequencies assignable to any cell in this set.
evidence: This describes the computational analysis approach.
